items.title: 69537_Jimmy Jones oral history interview
items.q: Tom Whaley -- Duke was living next door to me, and Tom Whaley was living about, oh, maybe three blocks away... So I had to take these scores over to Tom's to get them copied

ctx.x: But isn't that -- is there anybody else who would know? Understand what went with what and what belonged in some of the missing places and how it all fits together? I think (unaudible) was the one that told me that Duke used to write in kind of hieroglyphics. If you don't know what he means, he says, the average person, no matter how fine a musician he is, could walk up to an Ellington score and not know what it means.

Yes, that's right. That's very true, because there was one time I was doing some things with Johnny Hodges, you know, with a small group, about eight or ten pieces, and Tom Whaley -- Duke was living next door to me, and Tom Whaley was living about, oh, maybe three blocks away, and Billy Strayhorn. We were all living in one area. So I had to

take these scores over to Tom's to get them copied, and Tom says, "Take a look at this. This is one of Duke's scores." And I looked at it, and I said, "Tom, this can't work." He said, "You've been listening to it for the last 25 years."

items.title: 69537_Jimmy Jones oral history interview
items.q: Tom Whaley Wheeler, Duke's orchestrator, had a table off to the side, you know, and he was writing

ctx.x: And they did the whole album in one day. They had been on the road, you know, just passing through, and Tom Whaley Wheeler, Duke's orchestrator, had a table off to the side, you know, and he was writing, and -- now this was basically Ellington's date, because it was with his company, you know, the company he was signed with. And Duke wrote some -- he used some of the things out of, I think, "Paris Blues,"
that was one thing that he used that Louis Armstrong played in the picture.
